 The boundary between "need" and "want"
 DNCT - In the months leading up to Tet (Lunar New Year), the online shopping scene explodes like never before. With just a few taps on a phone screen, goods from all over the world can arrive at your doorstep within a few days.
 Báo Đà Nẵng • 15/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e Add Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e 0 The trend of online shopping is booming. Photo: Archival material. The convenience of e-commerce, coupled with a flurry of monthly discount events, especially at the end of the year, has drawn many people into a whirlwind of quick shopping – where the joy of "closing the deal" is often shorter than the time spent using the product.
 Order closing trap
 At this time of year, e-commerce platforms are entering their massive 11/11 and 12/12 sales events, as well as Lunar New Year promotions. All of this seems to be urging consumers to shop quickly, whether it's a little or a lot.
 At 11 PM, Nguyen Thi Minh Tam (24 years old, residing in Thanh Khe ward) was still engrossed in browsing TikTok and Shopee. The screen continuously displayed a barrage of live streams: "This item is almost sold out," "50% off voucher only 5 minutes left," "Biggest end-of-year sale." Unable to resist the feeling of "fear of missing out," Ms. Tam quickly clicked "Buy Now" on the ao dai (traditional Vietnamese dress) even though she already had several similar ones in her wardrobe.
 "Every time I get my salary or at the end of the year, my desire to treat myself increases. Whenever I see something pretty online with a deep discount, I immediately place an order. But the excitement only lasts until I open the box. Because there are some clothes and items I buy that I only use once and then put away, never touching again for a whole year," Ms. Tam confided.
 In the digital age, with the explosion of cashless payments and online shopping platforms, barriers to shopping have been virtually eliminated. Without the hassle of going to a store or worrying about cash, consumers can easily shop anywhere. This also makes them more susceptible to "uncontrolled shopping."
 And it's not just young people and women; even middle-aged men are "loyal" customers of e-commerce platforms.
 Mr. Pham Son (residing in Hoa Cuong ward) always rushes out to receive the delivery when he receives a phone call from the delivery person.
 You may also like "To avoid my wife and daughter seeing it and complaining, I've been growing vegetables on the rooftop lately. My phone keeps popping up with ads for seeds, fertilizers, and gardening supplies at very cheap prices. I've bought so much that my family is questioning it. Some things are usable, some aren't, but because they're cheap, I just buy them, thinking it doesn't cost me anything," Mr. Son confessed.
 However, the seeds didn't sprout and he couldn't ask anyone why, and the items made of poor quality materials couldn't be replaced because they were too cheap, not worth much. Gradually, Mr. Son's rooftop became a miniature "junkyard," causing his wife and daughter to constantly remind him to delete the shopping apps.
 Similarly, for many families, mini household items and dish racks that cost millions of dong are quickly sold for only a few hundred thousand dong on e-commerce platforms, but they lack the "luxury" feel.
 Fashion accessories, clothing for parents and children of poor quality, or trendy cosmetics are hoarded day after day, turning many corners of young people's rented rooms and apartments into wasteful "mini-warehouses" after each sale season.
 Shop wisely.
 The desire to shop for self-reward or stress relief intensifies during year-end shopping seasons. However, the confusion between "actual needs" and "impulsive emotions" is silently draining many people's wallets.
 Regarding this phenomenon, Ms. Tran Thi Chau, the owner of an online store specializing in household goods and food, shared that items on e-commerce platforms currently have a wide range of prices. The advertising of deep discounts and immediate order closing tactics leaves consumers with no time to carefully consider whether the purchase will be effective or not.
 "Buy first, then think about it later. Either way, you'll profit because the item is on sale. That's the mentality that makes buying cheap goods wasteful, even for branded items, because buyers don't really need them. They buy because they like them, because of the fear of missing out, or because it's cheaper than yesterday's price," Ms. Chau explained.
 “The algorithms of current shopping apps are designed to maximize the emotional stimulation of viewers, creating a feeling of excitement every time a user successfully completes a purchase. Especially during monthly or year-end sales, marketing messages that tap into the ‘cleaning up, replacing’ mentality further increase the desire to shop. This is the fast-paced consumer trap that causes many people to fall into a cycle of overspending beyond their financial means,” Ms. Chau added.
 You may also like Besides directly impacting your wallet, the habit of "buying what you like and replacing it when you get tired of it" also inadvertently creates a huge amount of waste for the environment, from plastic packaging and cardboard boxes to cheap plastic items and clothes that are discarded after only a few uses or even never used at all.
 To avoid getting caught in that "endless" shopping spree, Ms. Chau shared that people should apply the "48-Hour Rule." When wanting to buy an item that isn't on your current shopping list, add it to your cart and wait exactly 48 hours. After that time, if you still feel it's truly necessary, then proceed with the payment.
 Re-evaluating shopping habits isn't about extreme belt-tightening, but rather about developing a more mindful shopping habit, choosing truly quality items with long-term value instead of chasing short-term emotions and pleasures.
 From then on, your house won't be overflowing with unnecessary items, and your emotions won't depend on one or any particular product, where you only feel happy when you "close the deal"!
